claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC HEA nanoscale multilayers is controlled by the interplay between bulk dislocation activity and interface-mediated plasticity.
Decreasing the individual layer thickness at fixed total coating thickness increases interface density.
Higher interface density promotes a more distributed and gradual creep response.
Interfaces in these multilayers serve as barriers to dislocations.
Interfaces in these multilayers serve as dislocation sources.
Interfaces in these multilayers act as dislocation sinks.
Increasing interface density by reducing layer thickness suppresses bulk-like dislocation motion.
Suppression of bulk-like dislocation motion produces more uniform, controlled, and gradual plastic deformation.
Increasing layer thickness reduces the relative importance of interface-mediated plasticity.
Thicker layers promote bulk-like dislocation propagation and localized deformation.
Thicker layers cause an earlier onset of plasticity than thinner layers.
Thinner-layer multilayers will exhibit delayed localized deformation relative to thicker-layer multilayers.
Thicker-layer multilayers will exhibit earlier yield and localized plastic-deformation zones.
An intermediate layer thickness produces a balance between bulk and interface deformation mechanisms.
The proposed mechanism applies under moderate-temperature, sustained constant-stress loading.
A critical layer thickness may shift the balance between bulk and interface-mediated dislocation mechanisms.
